analysis.one_liner: Sets national standards for high-cost mortgages, bans single-premium credit insurance, and overrides state lending laws while expanding housing counseling.
analysis.headline: Introduced in December 2005 with zero cosponsors, the bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten federal rules for high-cost home loans: lenders would have to check that borrowers could actually repay without counting home equity, loan flipping would be banned, mandatory arbitration clauses and financed single-premium credit insurance would be prohibited, and borrowers would get new damages and rescission remedies. It also would have created a HUD Office of Housing Counseling with $75 million a year in grants. But the same bill would have wiped out state laws regulating mortgage lending — including rate caps and anti-abuse rules in states that had already passed stronger protections — and given loan buyers in the secondary market a safe harbor from borrower claims.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers taking out high-cost or subprime home loans would gain new federal protections: an ability-to-repay standard based on income rather than home equity, a ban on loan flipping without a net benefit, limits on prepayment penalties and late fees, a ban on mandatory arbitration, a ban on financing single-premium credit insurance into any home loan, an anti-steering rule, and larger damages ($500–$5,000 in individual suits, up to $1.5 million or 1% of a creditor's net worth in class actions). Nonprofit and government housing counseling organizations would gain $75 million per year in grants and a permanent HUD office. Mortgage lenders and secondary-market buyers would also gain, because the bill would preempt state lending laws and shield loan purchasers who follow stated policies from borrower claims.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High-cost mortgage borrowers and counseling nonprofits

how_it_helps.text: Lenders could not make a high-cost home loan unless a reasonable creditor would believe the borrower could make the payments based on income and obligations, not just home equity, with a rebuttable presumption when total monthly debts stay under 50% of gross income [S3].
The bill bans loan flipping — refinancing a loan made within the prior 36 months without a reasonable tangible net benefit — and prohibits prepayment penalties on high-cost loans entirely [S3].

Mandatory arbitration clauses would be barred in high-cost loans, preserving borrowers' right to sue in court, and lenders could not encourage default on an existing loan or charge fees to modify, renew, or extend a high-cost loan [S3].

On all home loans, not just high-cost ones, creditors could not finance single-premium credit insurance, could not steer borrowers into worse-priced loans than they qualify for, and prepayment penalties would be capped at 2.5% with a 36-month limit and a no-penalty loan option [S3].

Damages would rise for violations of the high-cost loan rules: $500 to $5,000 per individual action and class action recoveries up to the lesser of $1.5 million or 1% of the creditor's net worth, with the statute of limitations extended to two years [S3].

The bill creates a HUD Office of Housing Counseling, a toll-free counseling hotline, certified mortgage software, and authorizes $75 million per year for fiscal 2006 through 2009 in grants to states, local governments, and nonprofits for homeownership and rental counseling [S3].

analysis.who_pays: High-cost and subprime mortgage lenders and mortgage brokers would bear new compliance costs, lose fee income (payoff fees, modification fees, financed credit insurance), and face higher damages in lawsuits. Borrowers in states with stronger laws than the federal standard could lose those protections, because the bill preempts state rate limits and state rules on abusive lending practices. Loan buyers in the secondary market would face diligence obligations, though the bill gives them a safe harbor if they adopt policies against purchasing high-cost loans and sample-test loans rather than reviewing each one.
analysis.who_pays_short: Subprime lenders, brokers, and credit insurers

drawbacks.text: Section 106 preempts state laws regulating mortgage lending, including any state rate limitation and state rules on unfair, deceptive, or abusive lending practices — so in states with tougher anti-predatory-lending laws, the weaker federal standard would replace them [S3].

Loan purchasers and assignees get a broad safe harbor from borrower claims if they maintain policies barring high-cost loans, get seller warranties, and exercise due diligence that may be sampling-based rather than loan-by-loan review — weakening accountability for the investors who bought and securitized these loans [S3].

A new error-correction safe harbor would let creditors escape liability for violations of the high-cost loan rules, except knowing or intentional violations, by notifying the borrower and fixing the error within 45 days of closing or 60 days of discovery [S3].

The bill adds exceptions to existing bans on balloon payments and negative amortization for bridge loans, seasonal income schedules, and forbearance periods, expanding the circumstances in which risky loan structures are permitted [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill contained real, substantive protections for borrowers at the height of the pre-crisis subprime lending boom — an ability-to-repay standard, an anti-flipping rule, an arbitration ban, and a credit insurance ban on all home loans. But it is genuinely two bills in one: the same text would have preempted the stronger state lending laws that several states had already enacted and shielded secondary-market loan buyers from borrower claims. Whether borrowers came out ahead would have depended on which state they lived in and whether the new federal floor was stronger or weaker than their state's law — and the bill never advanced far enough for that trade-off to be tested in committee.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote, and died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. Wm. Lacy Clay introduced the Fair and Responsible Lending Act on December 8, 2005, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services [S1],[S5].
No other House member signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action for the remainder of the 109th Congress, which ended January 3, 2007 [S5].

The bill would have expanded federal protections for high-cost home loans — covering ability to repay, loan flipping, arbitration, credit insurance, and damages — while simultaneously preempting state mortgage lending laws [S3],[S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Subprime and high-cost mortgage lenders and brokers kept operating under the existing rules, facing neither the bill's new federal restrictions nor a national preemption of state laws. Borrowers gained nothing: no new federal protections passed, and the stronger state-level laws then in force stayed in place only because the federal preemption died with the bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Mortgage lenders; state laws stayed intact

sides.party_line_note: A single Democrat introduced the bill with zero cosponsors of either party, and it never reached a vote, so no partisan pattern of support or opposition is visible in the record.

industries.note: The bill would impose real new restrictions on high-cost lending — ability-to-repay, anti-flipping, arbitration and credit insurance bans, higher damages — but its Section 106 preemption would wipe out stricter state rate caps and anti-abuse laws, replacing a patchwork of state rules with a single national standard. The industry's interest in this bill runs against borrowers: its profits come from high fees and rates the federal rules target, while the preemption shields it from stronger state law.

industries.industry: Mortgage securitizers and secondary-market loan buyers
industries.note: The bill's preemption covers securitization, holding, and servicing of home loans, and its assignee provisions give purchasers a safe harbor from borrower claims if they maintain policies against high-cost loans and do sampling-based diligence. Investors who bought these loans would face less liability than under existing law.

The bill bans financing single-premium credit life, disability, unemployment, and property insurance into any home loan. These policies were added to loan balances and benefited the creditor as primary beneficiary, so eliminating them saves borrowers money and removes a revenue stream.

All broker compensation, direct and indirect, would count toward the points-and-fee triggers defining high-cost loans, and brokers would face a $5,000 penalty plus actual damages for steering borrowers into worse-priced loans than they qualify for.

The bill channels $75 million per year in HUD grants through certified nonprofit and government counseling organizations and makes HUD certification a condition of receiving counseling-related HUD assistance, building a permanent funding pipeline for the sector. Certified counselors also become gatekeepers for refinancing safe harbors under the loan-flipping rule.
